slides.title: The courier API answered in −2.7 seconds
slides.tldr: If the server clock is set back midway, "end − start" comes out negative. The assumption that a clock only moves forward is wrong.

blocks.body: Tina's dashboard shows the courier API's response time. One morning a row reads **−2.7 seconds**. In her code she simply subtracts the start time from the end time. But between those two lines, someone corrected the server's clock by turning it backwards. The fix is a clock that can't go backwards: [[time/clocks-lie/wall-vs-monotonic|the stopwatch]], two slides on.

marks.tip: microtime() reads the server's wall clock, which can jump forward or backward at any moment.
If the clock goes back 3 seconds in between, you get 0.3 − 3 = −2.7 here.
The deadline is tied to the wall clock. If the clock goes back an hour, this 5-second loop runs for an hour; if it jumps ahead, it stops at once.

blocks.caption: The real work took 0.3 seconds, yet the result is −2.7 seconds

actors.label: Tina's code
actors.tip: Reads the clock before and after the work, then subtracts.

actors.label: Server clock
actors.tip: The server's wall clock, which is right now 3 seconds ahead of real time.

actors.label: NTP
actors.tip: Corrects the server's clock by comparing it with a precise clock on the internet.

messages.label: You're 3 seconds ahead. Go back.
messages.tip: When the error is big, NTP fixes it in one jump rather than gradually.
Only 0.3 seconds really passed, but the reading is smaller than the earlier one.
A wrong number on a dashboard is a small loss. If someone feeds it into a sleep or a timeout, the program crashes or hangs.

blocks.body: A wall clock is for telling the time, not for measuring it.

aside.title: Cloudflare on New Year's night
aside.body: At midnight UTC on January 1, 2017, an extra second was added to the world's clocks. Cloudflare's DNS software assumed that subtracting two times could never give a number below zero. That night it did, the code crashed, and some customers' sites failed to load properly for hours.

items.meaning: The server's clock for date and time. When it gets corrected, it can jump.
Network Time Protocol: how a server keeps its clock in line with a precise one.

check.q: The real work took 0.3 seconds. How did the result come out as −2.7 seconds?
check.a: Between the two readings, the server's wall clock was set back 3 seconds. The second reading is smaller than the first, so the difference is 0.3 − 3 = −2.7.

slides.title: Four ways a clock lies
slides.tldr: Skew, drift, NTP jumps and leap seconds: for these four reasons two machines' clocks never match exactly, and even a single clock doesn't run in a straight line.

blocks.title: The clocks in a school's classrooms
blocks.body: Every classroom in a school has its own wall clock. One is two minutes fast, another a minute slow, because each clock runs a little quick or a little slow. Now and then the custodian listens to the radio's time signal and turns the hands to match, so the clock suddenly jumps. Each of your servers is one of those classroom clocks.

blocks.caption: Four kinds of clock error, at school and on servers

cells: Two rooms show two different times
Two servers differ by a few ms up to a few seconds
rows.tip: The difference between two machines' readings at the same moment. A few milliseconds when NTP is healthy; it can reach minutes when NTP is off.

cells: The clock creeps a little ahead every day
Left uncorrected, it wanders by seconds per day
rows.tip: A computer's clock counts the vibrations of a quartz crystal. They change with temperature and age, so every machine runs at its own pace.

cells: The custodian turns the hands to match
The clock suddenly jumps forward or back
rows.tip: For small errors NTP nudges the clock's speed up or down (slew). For big ones it corrects in one jump (step), and time can go backwards.

cells: A 61-second minute at the end of the year
23:59:60 appears, or the same second occurs twice
rows.tip: To keep UTC in step with the Earth's rotation, an extra second is occasionally added. The last one was at the end of 2016, and it has been decided to retire the leap second by 2035.

blocks.title: What this means in practice
items: Comparing timestamps from two servers to say "which came first" isn't safe.
On one server, a later reading can be smaller than an earlier one.
A user's phone or laptop clock can be wrong by hours.

items.meaning: The difference between two machines' clock readings at the same moment.
A single clock gradually running ahead of or behind real time.
NTP corrects small errors gradually (slew) and large ones in one jump (step).
Spreading the extra second over the whole day instead of adding it in one go. The big clouds do this.

items.desc: Check whether the clock is synced with NTP
See how far this server is from real time

items: Run NTP (chrony) on every server and alert on clock offset. That reduces the error but never makes it zero.
If a VM is paused for a while (pause or live migration), its clock can jump a long way when it wakes up.

check.q: What is the difference between skew and drift?
check.a: Skew is the difference between two clocks' readings at the same moment. Drift is one clock slowly wandering away from real time. Drift builds up into skew, and when NTP corrects it, the clock jumps.

slides.title: The wall clock vs the stopwatch
slides.tldr: A wall clock tells you what time it is and can jump. A monotonic clock only moves forward and tells you how long something took. Always use the second one to measure time.

blocks.title: The school track meet
blocks.body: In the 100-yard dash, the coach doesn't note the time from the wall clock; she holds a stopwatch. If the custodian turns the wall clock's hands mid-race, the stopwatch doesn't care. But a stopwatch can't tell you what time of day it is; it only says how long has passed. Computers have exactly these two kinds of clock.

columns.title: Wall clock
items: Question: what time is it?
PHP: time(), microtime(), new DateTimeImmutable()
Can jump forward or backward
Use: created_at, logs, showing people
columns.tip: The clock for knowing the date and time. NTP can correct it whenever it likes, so you can't trust the difference between two readings.

columns.title: Monotonic (stopwatch)
items: Question: how long did it take?
PHP: hrtime(true), in nanoseconds
Only moves forward, never back
Use: latency, timeouts, waits between retries
columns.tip: Time counted from some fixed point on the machine. It never goes backwards, so the difference between two readings is always right.

marks.tip: hrtime(true) returns an integer: how many nanoseconds have passed since some starting point. The number itself is not a date.
The difference between two readings can never be negative, even if NTP turns the clock.
This loop now runs for exactly 5 seconds, whatever happens to the wall clock.

blocks.body: When did it happen? Ask the wall clock. How long did it take? Ask the stopwatch.

aside.body: About to subtract two time readings? Both must come from hrtime().

items: Don't store an hrtime() value in the database or send it to another server. The number means something only on that one machine, during that one run.
The browser has the same split: `Date.now()` is the wall clock, `performance.now()` is the stopwatch.

items.meaning: Moving in only one direction. Here: a clock whose reading never decreases.

check.q: Why can't you fill created_at with an hrtime(true) value?
check.a: The number isn't a date. It is nanoseconds counted from an arbitrary point on that machine, and only the difference between two readings means anything. For a date and time you need the wall clock.

slides.title: Symfony Clock: handing time to your tests
slides.tldr: Instead of calling new DateTimeImmutable() directly, inject a ClockInterface. In tests, use MockClock to freeze time and move it forward as you like.

blocks.body: An OTP is valid for 5 minutes. To test that, do you sit in the test for 5 minutes? If your code calls `new DateTimeImmutable()` itself, time is out of your control. The fix: make the clock a service and inject it from outside. In the real app Symfony supplies the real clock; in tests you supply a fake one.

blocks.caption: The same expiry test, without and with an injected clock

columns.title: new DateTimeImmutable() inside
items: The test really waits 5 minutes
Or you edit rows by hand to fake the time
The 299 s / 300 s boundary stays untested
columns.tip: The class reads the system clock itself, so a test cannot move time. It can only wait or fake the data.

columns.title: Injected ClockInterface
items: One call moves the clock 299 seconds
Both sides of the boundary run in milliseconds
Same result on every run
columns.tip: The class asks the clock it was given. The test hands it a MockClock and moves time itself.

marks.tip: Symfony autowires the real clock here by itself. You don't write any config.
There is only one way to learn the time: the injected clock. So changing the clock in a test changes time for the whole class.
MockClock is a frozen clock. Unless you say so, its time doesn't move by a single microsecond, so the test gives the same result every run.
sleep() and modify() only change the internal time. A 5-minute expiry gets tested in a few milliseconds.

blocks.body: Code that looks at the clock itself can't be tested. Hand it the clock from outside.

items.desc: See which ClockInterface will be autowired

items: In a WebTestCase or KernelTestCase, use `ClockSensitiveTrait` and call `static::mockTime()` to fake the clock for the whole app.
Don't write `new DateTimeImmutable()` in an entity's constructor. Pass in `$clock->now()` from a service.
Symfony's `MonotonicClock` runs on `hrtime()` inside, so its `now()` never goes backwards within one process.

check.q: When you call MockClock's sleep(299), does the test actually pause for 299 seconds?
check.a: No. MockClock just moves its internal time forward by 299 seconds. So a 5-minute expiry gets tested in a few milliseconds.

slides.title: Ordering events by comparing two servers' timestamps
slides.tldr: If server A's clock runs 80 ms ahead, a cancel that happens later gets a smaller timestamp than the create that happened earlier. For ordering, you need numbers, not timestamps.

blocks.body: An order is created on server A and canceled 50 milliseconds later on server B. A's clock is 80 ms ahead. Sort the report by timestamp and it shows the order was **canceled before it was created**. Just as you can't tell who walked in first by comparing two classroom clocks, you can't do it by comparing two servers' clocks.

blocks.caption: Create really came first, cancel second, but the timestamps say the opposite

actors.label: Server A
actors.tip: Its clock is 80 ms ahead of real time.

actors.label: Events table
actors.tip: Both servers write rows here, each stamping its own clock's time.

messages.label: created — 10:00:00.080
messages.tip: Real time is 10:00:00.000. A wrote the time from its own clock, which runs ahead.

messages.label: canceled — 10:00:00.050
messages.tip: Real time is 10:00:00.050, which is 50 ms after the create.
The cancel's timestamp is 30 ms smaller than the create's. Code that trusts this order will make the wrong decision.

blocks.title: Which clock for which job
items: How long did it take (latency, timeouts): `hrtime()`, the stopwatch.
When did it happen (created_at, logs): UTC time taken from `ClockInterface`.
Which came first: a version or sequence number, not a timestamp.
Has it expired: only the server's clock, never the user's phone.

marks.tip: One database numbers the rows in the order it receives them. One authority means no two clocks to compare.
Keep the time for display and reports. Never sort or decide by it when events come from different servers.
Sorting by id gives one agreed order: created, then canceled. The price: it is the order of arrival at this database, and it needs one place that hands out numbers.

items: Don't make decisions based on a `createdAt` sent from a mobile app. Users can change their phone's clock themselves.
Even on one server, two rows can have exactly the same `created_at`. Add `id` when you sort.

items.label: Which came first: the right way

check.q: A's clock is 80 ms ahead. An event happens on A, and another on B 50 ms later. Sorted by timestamp, which one appears first?
check.a: B's event. A's event carries a time 80 ms too high, so B's event, which happened 50 ms later, gets a timestamp 30 ms smaller.

slides.title: The newer edit vanished
slides.tldr: If you pick the "latest" write by comparing two machines' clock times, the stale write from the clock that runs ahead wins, and the genuinely newer write is silently lost.

blocks.title: Two branches, two wall clocks
blocks.body: Two bank branches each have a wall clock, and one runs 5 minutes fast. Both branches update the same customer's address, and head office rules: "the later time wins". The older update from the fast clock wins. You simply can't tell by looking at clocks which change really happened last.

blocks.caption: Phone A's clock is 5 minutes fast, so the older edit wins; counting versions fixes it

actors.label: Phone A
actors.tip: Its clock is 5 minutes fast. It changes the name at 10:00 real time.

actors.label: Phone B
actors.tip: Its clock is correct. It changes the name at 10:02 real time, which is after A.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Decides which write is "latest" by the timestamp that comes with each one.

messages.label: name = Ryan, time 10:05
messages.tip: Real time is 10:00, but A's fast clock wrote 10:05.

messages.label: name = Ryan Miller, time 10:02
messages.tip: This is really the newer change, but its timestamp is smaller.
The database threw away the newer change without any error. Nobody ever finds out.

messages.note: Fix: versions. A saves v4, B saves v5
messages.tip: The server hands out the numbers, so no phone clock is involved. B had loaded v4, so its change lands on top as v5. Had B loaded v3, the server would answer 409 instead of silently dropping one edit.

aside.title: The story of the synced notes
aside.body: A notes app synced a phone and a laptop by looking at clock times. One user's laptop clock was wrong, so the notes they had just written kept being overwritten by older versions.

items.meaning: Of two changes, keep the one with the larger timestamp and drop the other.
The relationship of knowing that one event caused, or came before, another. It is not clock time.

check.q: Phone A's clock is 5 minutes fast. A wrote first, B wrote later. Whose write does LWW keep, and why is that wrong?
check.a: A's, because its timestamp, 10:05, is larger. But B's write is the genuinely newer one, and it is lost without any error.

slides.title: Logical clocks: counting cause and effect, not time
slides.tldr: Each machine keeps its own counter. It travels with every message, and on receipt the receiver sets its counter to max(own, received) + 1. So causes come first and effects after.

blocks.body: If clock time can't be trusted, how do you order events? Lamport's answer: drop the clock and keep a plain **counter**. There are two rules. When you do something yourself, add 1 to the counter. When you receive a message from someone else, set the counter to `max(your own, the message's) + 1`. So anything known to have happened earlier always has a smaller number.

blocks.caption: Lamport clock: the counter travels with messages and pulls the receiver forward

actors.label: Server A
actors.tip: Keeps its own counter, starting at 0.

actors.label: Server B
actors.tip: Keeps its own separate counter, starting at 0.

messages.tip: When it does something itself, the counter goes up by 1.

messages.label: Message, counter 1
messages.tip: When sending, it attaches its own counter.
On receipt, B's counter becomes 2. That is larger than event X's 1, which proves X came first.
C's counter is 3, later than both X (1) and B's event (2).

blocks.body: If X happens before Y, then counter(X) < counter(Y). The reverse is not always true.

aside.body: For two events with no message path between them (concurrent), a smaller or larger counter does not mean "earlier" or "later". A Lamport clock can't tell them apart.

items: If you want a single total order of all events, break ties on equal counters with the node id: (counter, node id).
To detect concurrent events you need a vector clock. It is heavier, and is used for conflict detection in databases.

check.q: Server B's counter is 0 and it receives a message with counter 5 from A. What is B's new counter, and why?
check.a: 6. The rule is max(own 0, received 5) + 1 = 6. That shows the receipt happened after the send.

slides.title: Ordering work: version numbers and sequences
slides.tldr: Give every entity its own version number and increment it atomically with each change. Drop any event whose version is smaller than what you already have. No clock needed.

blocks.body: In real systems the simple way is to create the order in one place: the database. Each change increments `version` by one, and the change event carries that number. A consumer accepts only a number larger than the latest version it knows. A stale event that arrives late does no harm. The price: one place has to hand out the numbers, so this suits one entity in one database; several databases need the other tools on the next slide.

blocks.code:
-- the change and the new version together, atomically; PostgreSQL
UPDATE customer
SET name = :name, version = version + 1
WHERE id = :id
RETURNING version;

marks.tip: Bumping the version and changing the name happen in one statement. If two requests arrive together, each gets a different number.
The new version comes back. This is what goes into the event.
It writes only if the version is higher. Events arriving in the wrong order still end up with the right result.
A result of 0 means the event is stale and nothing changed. It is not an error, so it is safe to ignore.

items: PostgreSQL sequence numbers are handed out in the order transactions ask for them, not in COMMIT order. So if you read "everything after N" with a cursor, a smaller number that commits after a bigger one can be missed.
UUIDv7 and ULID sort by time, but across machines they depend on the clocks. They give an approximate order, not proof of cause and effect.

items.label: The version column in optimistic locking

check.q: The version 7 event arrives first, then version 6 arrives late. What should the result be, and how?
check.a: The state stays at version 7. `WHERE version < 6` doesn't match (the row has 7), so 0 rows change and the stale event is dropped.

slides.title: Four ways to order events, and when to use each
slides.tldr: Clocks are approximate; Lamport gives cause and effect; version numbers create order in one place; a hybrid logical clock reads like a clock and also respects cause and effect.

blocks.body: Each of the four answers a different question. A **hybrid logical clock (HLC)** keeps the wall-clock time and adds a small counter to preserve cause and effect: (clock time, counter). If the clock goes backwards, it increments the counter and moves on. Most apps write to a single database, and there version numbers are enough.

blocks.caption: Four ways to establish order, side by side

cells: The clock can be wrong; order isn't certain
rows.tip: Great for showing time in logs or reports. Not reliable for deciding what came first.
Just a counter: cheap and simple. But you can't read real time from the counter.
One database or one leader hands out the numbers. The simplest option, and enough for most apps.
Multi-region databases use it. App developers don't usually build it; they get it inside the database.

blocks.body: Which came first is a job for numbers, not clocks. Clocks are only for showing people the time.

use: One database, one entity's history: version numbers
Many regions, local writes: HLC or the database's built-in support
avoid: Using a client-sent time to decide order

check.q: Which clock can be read like clock time and also respects cause-and-effect order?
check.a: The hybrid logical clock (HLC). It keeps a (clock time, counter) pair, and if the clock goes backwards it bumps the counter to preserve the order.

slides.title: How to get rid of last-write-wins
slides.tldr: Choosing the "newer" write by the client's updatedAt lets stale writes overwrite newer ones. Detect conflicts by comparing versions, and merge fields one at a time.

marks.tip: The client's updatedAt is the client's clock time. A clock that runs ahead always wins.
The whole row is replaced, so changes someone else made to other fields are silently wiped out.
Checks that the version the client saw when it made its change still equals the row's version (the entity needs a #[ORM\Version] column). No clock needed.
Write only the changed fields and leave the rest as they are. Unrelated changes then don't erase each other.
On a conflict, tell the client. Have it fetch the new data and merge, or ask the user to choose.

items: LWW is fine where losing a write costs nothing: a cache, a "last seen" time. Not for money, addresses or documents.
Never base a decision on the client's time. If you need a time, use the server's time or a server-assigned version.

check.q: Instead of picking the "newer" write by the client's updatedAt, what do you use to detect a conflict, and what do you do when one happens?
check.a: A server-assigned version. If it doesn't match, return 409 so the client can fetch the new data and merge, or let the user choose.

slides.title: The meeting suddenly moved by an hour
slides.tldr: Store a London user's "every Monday at 10 am" meeting in UTC and it slides to 11 am after the DST change, with no bug in the code.

blocks.body: Sarah, in London, creates a weekly meeting in February: "every Monday at 10 am". The app stores the first date in UTC and builds every later Monday by adding exactly 7 days (168 hours). On March 29 the clocks in London go forward an hour (DST begins), and the meeting suddenly shows up at 11 am in Sarah's calendar. The UTC time is still correct, but it isn't what Sarah asked for.

blocks.caption: The same UTC time looks different on London clocks in February and April

rows.tip: In winter London time equals UTC (GMT), so everything looks right here.
The last Monday before DST begins. Still no trouble.
London is now UTC+1 hour (BST, British Summer Time). The same UTC time shows the meeting at 11, an hour off without Sarah ever agreeing to it.

blocks.body: For a future local event, store "I want 10 am", not UTC.

aside.title: The medicine reminder
aside.body: A health app stored its "medicine every night at 9" reminder in UTC. On the day the country changed its clocks, the reminder moved to 10 pm, and users complained about their medication times.

items: Arizona (except the Navajo Nation) has no DST and stays on UTC-7, so a team there won't notice this problem. Users in Europe and most of the US will.

check.q: You store the reminder "every night at 9" in UTC and add 24 hours each day. What happens after the DST change, and why?
check.a: The time shifts by an hour on the user's clock. UTC has no DST, but the user's local clock moves forward or back an hour.

slides.title: Two kinds of time: the instant and the wall clock
slides.tldr: Store a moment that has happened in UTC. Store a future local event as the local time plus the zone name (Europe/London), not as an offset.

blocks.title: A video call with your brother abroad
blocks.body: A brother in New York and a brother in London talked yesterday at one exact moment. The moment was one, yet their clocks showed different times. That is "a moment in the past", and it is stored in UTC. But "a call every Monday at 10 am London time next month" is a wall-clock time plus a place's rules. That is stored just as it is: local time and place.

blocks.caption: How to store each kind of time

columns.title: A moment that happened
items: Store in UTC: timestamptz
Convert to the user's zone when displaying
Examples: paid_at, created_at
columns.tip: Order created, payment, login, logs. It happened once, so it is one fixed instant.

columns.title: A future local event
items: Local time (no zone) + the zone name
Work out the UTC each time, using the rules of that day
Example: 10:00 + Europe/London
columns.tip: A meeting, a reminder, a shop's opening time. It follows people's clocks, and the rules can change later.

blocks.body: The past: UTC. A future local event: local time + zone name.

items.meaning: The difference in hours from UTC, such as +01:00. It is true for one moment only.
A place name that carries the complete rules, like Europe/London or America/New_York. It holds the DST history and future rules.

items: "+01:00" is not a stored zone. When DST ends London's offset changes, but the stored "+01:00" stays.
Governments sometimes change DST rules. If you store the zone name, a tzdata update fixes future events too.

check.q: Which should be stored in UTC and which as "local time + zone": (a) a payment was made, (b) a meeting every Monday at 10 am in London?
check.a: (a) UTC, because it is a moment that has happened. (b) Local 10:00 plus the name Europe/London, because a future local event follows the DST rules.

slides.title: The DST gap and the doubled hour
slides.tldr: In spring one hour of local time doesn't exist (a gap); in autumn one hour happens twice (an overlap). Put an event in that time and the code quietly guesses; detect both cases and decide on purpose.

blocks.body: In London on March 29, 2026, at 1 am the clock jumps straight to 2 am. So **01:30 simply doesn't exist**. On October 25 the clock goes from 2 am back to 1 am, so **01:30 happens twice**. Ask for something to happen in those moments, and the code either moves it by guesswork or picks the earlier or the later one, and you never get told. The fix is to list every real moment that could match the wall time, then choose.

blocks.caption: The two DST boundaries in London, 2026

rows.tip: In spring the clocks go forward. Every local time between 01:00 and 02:00 is nonexistent.
In autumn the clocks go back. 01:00-02:00 happens once in BST and again in GMT: the same numbers, two different moments.

marks.tip: Invalid input raises no error; the time just moves an hour. The user never knows.
It picks one of the two possible moments, silently, and the choice can change with the PHP version. The other can never come out.
Around a DST change the zone has two offsets (+00:00 and +01:00). Try both and see which UTC moments produce the wall time you were given.
Zero candidates: the time falls in the gap. Two candidates: it is in the overlap. One: an ordinary time.
You choose the rule on purpose. A gap is refused, so the user can pick another time; an overlap needs the earlier-or-later flag.

blocks.title: What the fixed version does
items: A gap gives zero candidates: refuse it and ask the user for another time (or pick a rule, such as the next valid time).
An overlap gives two: you choose the earlier or the later one, then store it in UTC.
For daily jobs, don't use "+24 hours"; use `modify('+1 day')` in the local zone.

aside.body: Adding hours to a local time is one thing; adding days is another. Do day arithmetic in the local zone.

items: In tests, keep at least two cases for 01:30 on March 29 and on October 25.

check.q: Why is "01:30" on October 25, 2026 in London ambiguous, and how does storing UTC settle it?
check.a: That day 01:00-02:00 happens twice (BST and GMT). In UTC they become two distinct moments (00:30 or 01:30 UTC), so it is clear which one you mean.

slides.title: Storing and computing: SQL and PHP
slides.tldr: Past moments go in timestamptz. Future events get the local time plus the zone name, and a separately computed next_run_at (UTC) for the scheduler.

marks.tip: timestamptz stores UTC internally and displays it in the session's zone. The name is misleading: it doesn't actually store a zone.
Never put +01:00 in this column; put the place name. The name gives you the correct offset for any date.
Useful for the scheduler. It is always a value computed from local_start and timezone.
Attaching the zone name to the time makes PHP pick the right offset (GMT or BST) for that date.
modify() works in the local zone, so the wall clock doesn't change. Adding 168 hours in UTC would have shifted across DST.
Convert to UTC at the very end, and write that to next_run_at. The scheduler compares only against UTC.

items: Keep PHP's default timezone at UTC (`date.timezone = UTC`) and pass an explicit DateTimeZone wherever you need a zone.
After each run, compute the next one from that moment and rewrite next_run_at.
Validate the zone name: `in_array($z, DateTimeZone::listIdentifiers(), true)`.

check.q: To find the next date of a weekly local meeting, why add `+1 week` in the local zone rather than 168 hours in UTC?
check.a: Adding in the local zone keeps the wall clock (10:00) intact, even when DST changes. Adding hours in UTC shifts the local time by an hour after DST.

slides.title: Displaying: in the user's zone, in Vue
slides.tldr: The API sends UTC (ISO 8601, ending in Z); in Vue, Intl.DateTimeFormat formats it in the user's own zone. For an event elsewhere, show the event's own zone too.

blocks.body: Let the server always send times in one format: ISO 8601 in UTC, ending in `Z`. The browser knows where the user is, so display is the client's job. `Intl.DateTimeFormat` follows DST rules by itself. For an event in another city (say a London meeting), show both zones side by side so nobody gets confused.

marks.tip: The UTC string from the API. Without the trailing Z, the browser will wrongly take it as local time.
Passing timeZone makes Intl follow that zone's DST rules and give the right local time. No adding or subtracting hours by hand.
The user's browser zone, such as America/New_York. You can also store it on the server as a separate setting.

blocks.title: Rules for sending from Symfony
items: Entity times are DateTimeImmutable; before export, call `setTimezone(new DateTimeZone('UTC'))`.
In JSON use RFC 3339 / ISO 8601 (the Serializer's default). Don't build date strings by hand.
In emails or SMS, format the time in the user's zone and include the zone name.
`new Date('2026-04-06 09:00')`, a string without a zone, is assumed to be in the browser's local zone. Always send a string with `Z` or an offset.
Writing email times in the server's timezone gives users in other countries the wrong time.
For schedules like cron, the server's zone (usually UTC) is a separate matter: for a user's local event, drive it from next_run_at in UTC.

check.q: What can go wrong in Vue if the API sends the time as `2026-04-06 09:00`, without the trailing Z?
check.a: The browser treats it as the user's own local time, not UTC, so the displayed time is wrong. To say UTC, you must add `Z` or an offset.

slides.title: The phone's clock said the OTP had expired
slides.tldr: If expiry is decided by the client's clock, a fast clock cancels a valid code and a slow clock lets an expired one through. The server decides.

blocks.title: The train ticket and the station clock
blocks.body: The ticket says "train leaves 10:05". Whatever the passenger's wristwatch says, the train leaves by the station's clock. The passenger thinks "there's still time", but the conductor closes the doors. Expiry works the same way: the server's clock decides what is still valid.

blocks.caption: A phone clock an hour fast "expires" a fresh OTP; sending it anyway lets the server judge

actors.label: User's phone
actors.tip: Its clock is wrong, an hour ahead of real time.

actors.label: Server
actors.tip: Its clock is synced via NTP. It is the real authority on expiry.

messages.label: OTP 4821, valid until 10:05
messages.tip: Issued at 10:00 real time. It is valid for 5 minutes.
The phone thinks it expired 56 minutes ago. The real time is 10:01.

messages.note: Shows "code expired", never sends it to the server
messages.tip: The app never gave the server a chance. The user is stuck.
A valid code was wasted by a decision made on the client's clock.

messages.label: Fix: send 4821 anyway
messages.tip: The app no longer judges expiry. It just passes the code on.

messages.label: Server clock 10:01 < 10:05: accepted
messages.tip: The server compares expires_at with its own synced clock, so the fast phone clock changes nothing.

blocks.body: Expiry is decided on the server's clock. The client only displays.

aside.title: The user changed "today's date"
aside.body: A trial app counted 30 days from the phone's date. Anyone who set the phone's date back could use the trial forever. The reverse happens too: if the phone's date is wrong, an innocent user's trial ends early.
The client's clock is untrustworthy, so never use it for a security decision.

check.q: Why does the app say the OTP has "expired" before the server does when the phone's clock runs fast, and what is the right design?
check.a: The app computes expiry from its own wrong clock. In the right design the server checks expiry, and the client just shows a countdown from the remaining time the server gave it.

slides.title: Deadline vs duration: what to store, what to count
slides.tldr: Store expiry as a fixed moment (a deadline, expires_at). To count down or measure a wait, use a duration and a monotonic timer.

blocks.body: Expiry can be expressed in two different ways. A **deadline** is a fixed moment: "invalid after 10:05:00 UTC". A **duration** is a length of time: "300 seconds". A deadline is better for storing expiry, because everyone sees the same moment. Store a duration and you must also remember separately when it started. For counting down or measuring a timeout, on the other hand, a duration and a monotonic timer are the right tools.

blocks.caption: Deadline vs duration: which goes where

rows.tip: The same information in two shapes. At issue time, turn the ttl into a deadline and store that.

cells: In the database, in a token
rows.tip: With the deadline in the database, "is it valid now?" is a simple query. A cache removes entries by their length by itself.
When measuring a duration, a clock jump in between does no harm. A monotonic clock never goes backwards.

cells: Send the seconds left; don't make it compute
rows.tip: The server says "297 seconds left", and the client counts down on its own stopwatch. The phone's date isn't needed.

blocks.body: Store expiry as a deadline; measure time with a duration and a monotonic timer.

items.meaning: Time to live: how long something is allowed to stay alive.
A clock that only moves forward, never back. For measuring time, not for knowing the date.

check.q: To show a countdown, do you send expires_at or the seconds remaining, and how does the client count?
check.a: The server sends the seconds remaining. The client subtracts using `performance.now()` (monotonic), so the countdown stays right even if the phone's date is wrong.

slides.title: The server is the judge, with a small grace
slides.tldr: Compare expires_at with the current time from the server's Clock. Allow a small grace for network delay and slight clock differences between issue and verification.

blocks.body: Why a grace at all? The code is valid until 10:05:00. Rachel taps Send at 10:04:59.8, but the request crawls over a weak mobile network and reaches the server at 10:05:00.4. With no grace, someone who was on time is told "expired". A few seconds of grace forgives that delay. The price: a stolen code lives that much longer, so keep it tiny in security code.

marks.tip: Grace covers only technical gaps: a few seconds. It is not a way to extend the expiry.
hash_equals avoids timing attacks. And if the code doesn't match, stop right here.
The time comes from ClockInterface, so a test can use MockClock to pass the expiry. The client's clock never comes into it.
performance.now() is monotonic; it keeps the same pace even if the phone's date changes.
It works out the seconds left from elapsed time, not the phone's Date. It is only for display; the decision is the server's.

items: In JWT verification, a library's `leeway` or clock-skew setting is the same idea. Usually 5-30 seconds.
Business grace is a different thing: keeping the service on for 3 days after a subscription ends. That is policy; give it a clear name in code (graceUntil).
Make the grace very large and the expiry means nothing. Keep it small in security code.

check.q: An OTP arrives 5 minutes 1 second after issue, with a 5-second grace. Why is it accepted, and why would a 5-minute grace be wrong?
check.a: 5 seconds is enough to cover technical delay and slight clock differences, so it is accepted. With a 5-minute grace, the expiry doubles and security is weakened.

slides.title: Timeout budget: spending the whole request's time in portions
slides.tldr: Instead of a separate timeout on every call, set one total deadline for the whole request. Count it with hrtime and give each step only what remains.

blocks.body: In an order request the client won't wait more than 3 seconds. Inside, the database, the payment gateway and the email queue are all involved. Give each one its own "10 seconds" timeout and the total gets out of hand. So treat the 3 seconds in total as a budget, subtract the cost at each step, and don't start more work once the budget is spent.

blocks.caption: A 3000 ms budget, divided by step

items.label: Total budget
items.tip: The longest the client will wait. If it takes longer, the client gives up first.

items.label: Database
items.tip: An ordinary query; a small part of the budget.

items.label: Payment gateway
items.tip: The slowest step, so the biggest share. Its timeout can't be given more than this.

items.label: Email to queue
items.tip: Only sending a message, not the email itself. Fast.

items.label: Left (safety)
items.tip: Kept for the network, serialization and unexpected slowness.

marks.tip: hrtime(true) is monotonic, so the budget is counted correctly even if the clock jumps.
In HttpClient, a max_duration of 0 or less means unlimited. So check whether the budget is spent first.
Each call has its own limit (1.5s) but never more than the remaining budget. Whichever is smaller applies.

items.meaning: The idle timeout: how long to wait when no data arrives. Not the total time.
The maximum total time for the whole request + response, in seconds.

items: Tell internal services the remaining budget in a header (for example `X-Deadline-Ms`) so they can keep count too.

check.q: What is the difference between `timeout` and `max_duration` in HttpClient, and which do you need to hold a budget?
check.a: `timeout` is the idle time when no data arrives; `max_duration` is the total limit for the whole request. To hold a total budget you need `max_duration`.

slides.title: Three timeout traps: bigger inside, retries multiply, unbounded
slides.tldr: If an inner timeout is bigger than the outer one, work carries on after the outer caller has given up. Retries multiply the timeout. Without a timeout, one hung call blocks everything.

blocks.body: The client gives up after 3 seconds. But inside the server, the gateway call has a 10-second timeout with 3 retries on top: 40 seconds in the worst case. The client has gone, yet the server keeps working, and the work may even succeed in the end. The user never finds out what happened. The third trap is a call with no sensible timeout at all: if the gateway hangs, each PHP worker that calls it just waits. With 20 workers, 20 stuck requests are enough for the whole site to stop answering.

blocks.code:
framework:
    http_client:
        scoped_clients:
            gateway.client:
                base_uri: '%env(GATEWAY_URL)%'
                timeout: 10         # idle only; no total limit
                retry_failed:
                    max_retries: 3  # 4 attempts × 10 seconds = 40 seconds

marks.tip: 10 seconds is bigger than the client's 3. The work carries on inside long after the outside has given up.
Every retry gets the full timeout again. The worst-case time multiplies.

blocks.code:
framework:
    http_client:
        scoped_clients:
            gateway.client:
                base_uri: '%env(GATEWAY_URL)%'
                timeout: 0.5
                max_duration: 0.8   # total limit per attempt
                retry_failed:
                    max_retries: 2
                    delay: 100
                    multiplier: 2   # 3 × 0.8 + 0.3 = 2.7 seconds < 3

marks.tip: There is a limit, and the worst case is 2.7 seconds in total, inside the client's 3.
Retries are few and bounded. Only idempotent calls are safe to retry; a charge call isn't, without an idempotency key.

blocks.title: Three rules
items: All the inner timeouts together must be smaller than the outer timeout.
Work out the worst-case total time of the retries first.
Every outbound call gets an explicit timeout; never rely on the default.
A timeout doesn't mean the work wasn't done. The gateway may have taken the money and only the reply never came. The outcome is "unknown", not "failed".

items.label: After a timeout: "I don't know whether it happened"

check.q: The client waits 3 seconds. Each attempt of the inner call takes at most 1 second, with 2 retries. Is that safe?
check.a: Almost: 3 attempts × 1 second = 3 seconds, and the retry delays on top push it past the limit. Shorten each attempt (say to 0.8) to stay within 3 seconds in total.
